1:
Whom Job is told to call on is the first quarrel. Gill allows two readings: call upon God, sound advice were it not ironical, or call over the roll of good men. Clarke hears the irony, asking what succour can come from those whose foundations are in the dust, and makes the holy ones creatures as dependent as Job himself, able to do nothing but as God directs: can the channel afford water once the fountain stops? Delitzsch makes them angels outright, as in Psalms 89, and finds in the rejected appeal the prologue's assumption that spirits good and bad are mixed into human affairs. Henry keeps them human, noting that the Old Testament has its saints too. Wesley puts the taunt bluntly: fools and wicked men may be found to defend Job, not one child of God. Ellicott notes only the turn to a personal tone, insinuating that its hearer is unwise and silly.

Whose wrath does the killing is the second. Gill offers three: the wrath is God's and consumes like fire, or the man's own passion risen so high he dies in the fit, or the rage that drives him to acts fetching death from God or the magistrate. Henry chooses the second and turns it on Job: quarrelling with God he injures himself most, anger at his losses and envy at his friends' ease only adding to the pain; Henry also catches the cruelty, Job having told his wife she spoke as the foolish women and hearing now that he acts as the foolish men. Clarke treats the line as a maxim the experience of ages established, that wrath falls only on the impious, so that Job cannot be other; and he observes that fool, silly and simple are Solomon's epithets, which some take as an argument for his hand in the book. Wesley hears the whole accusation in it, envy at prospering sinners and wrath against God together.

The flourishing that was cursed is granted only to be withdrawn. Gill explains why the prosperity is conceded at all: to forestall the objection that the wicked are notoriously not in trouble as other men. Wesley has the man not merely prosperous but apparently secured for the future, the curse read off afterwards from the event. Ellicott renders the cursing as a confident declaration, stated distinctly and without hesitation, and hears the insinuation underneath: manifest misery argues secret unsoundness. Clarke says he knew from God's dealings that such men must soon be blasted and so ventured to pronounce the doom. Henry alone separates foresight from desire: Eliphaz did not pray for the ruin but prognosticated it, having gone into the sanctuary to learn their end. No soul prospers, he adds, that takes root in the earth.

The children and the harvest follow, and one word of the fifth verse divides everybody. Henry reads an invidious glance at Job, the children thinking themselves safe in their eldest brother's house and crushed instead in a gateway perhaps built highest and falling heaviest. Clarke supplies the custom, the tribunal sitting at the city gate, and passes on the Targum's reading, that they are bruised in the gate of hell at the great judgment. Ellicott would rather they crush one another, ruined by their own rivalries like a house divided. Gill gives the harvest to hungry heirs kept bare or to the poor the man had oppressed. Then the last clause: Clarke argues for the thirsty rather than the robber, since what follows is swallowing, and spends his longest note on the starved desert banditti, citing Volney on legs of tendon without calf and six dates a day; Ellicott suspects a trap or a snare, noting old versions that read the thirsty and so complete the parallel; Delitzsch has an intriguer snatching at the wealth. Henry simply names the Sabeans, against whom a hedge of thorns proved nothing.
6:
Where trouble comes from opens the next movement. Gill observes that the word for affliction also means iniquity, so Aben Ezra reads both clauses of moral rather than natural evil; sin cannot spring from the dust God made, which yields bread and oil. Henry takes the denial as a statement about providence: prosperity and adversity are not proportioned as exactly as day and night, but as God thinks fit; and on the alternative rendering, bad men may not blame the soil, the climate or the stars. Clarke turns it to accusation: without an adequate cause Job could not be so grievously afflicted. The sparks then divide them. Clarke abandons the received rendering for the sons of the coal lifting up their flight, bold men who rise above their trials; Coverdale had the bird instead. Wesley hears only how natural affliction is, and asks why we should be surprised at it as strange; Henry makes transgressions the sparks thrown from the furnace of original corruption.

Then the advice, with a reproof folded inside it. Gill reads the particle as an assertion, truly I do seek unto God: the counsel describes what Eliphaz did under lighter troubles of his own. Clarke paraphrases: were I in your place, instead of irritating my soul with useless complaints, I would apply to my Maker. Henry hears the tacit rebuke and then undercuts it, remarking that it is easy to say what we would do in another's case and the trial often proves it not so easy; whence his rule, that we give a friend no counsel we would not take ourselves. Delitzsch reads the catalogue that follows as chosen designedly, God bringing down haughtiness and pitying those who need it.

The doxology is weighed differently by each hand. Henry works the three epithets: unsearchable, so that the wisest philosophers confess themselves at a loss and none may judge works above inquiry; numberless, his power never spent; marvellous, eternity hardly long enough to admire them. Wesley says the excursus exists to show the disproportion between God and Job. Gill spreads the great things over creation, providence and grace. On the rain Clarke prefers the Chaldee, localising it to Israel and the provinces of the peoples, and reads fields as ridged plots, none left without its due moisture. Henry thinks rain was chosen because its commonness makes men reckon it a little thing; Wesley finds the wonder in a heavy body hung in air and distributed as God sees fit; Gill adds that no Gentile vanity can give it. Ellicott draws the doctrine of the eleventh verse, that exaltation must come from God and not from vain striving, comparing Hannah's prayer.

The crafty and the poor close it. Gill passes on a Jewish reading making the rain itself the agent, defeating hoarders who raise the price of corn in a drought and must now sell cheap, and the Targum's Egyptians plotting against Israel. Henry prefers history, naming Ahithophel, Sanballat and Haman; Ellicott notes Paul quoting the verse to the Corinthians, and that froward means crooked, Naphtali deriving from the same root. Clarke finds the pit-digger's proverb universal, quoting Lucretius. Over the daytime darkness Ellicott suspects the Egyptian plague that might be felt, calling it a possible note of date and one of many slight contacts with the Pentateuch, while Wesley and Gill read plain infatuation. The sword from their mouth is contested: Clarke calls the construction harsh and prefers eleven manuscripts reading the sword of their mouth, with the Chaldee and Vulgate agreeing; Ellicott dismisses it as grammatical nicety and dwells instead on God as the Saviour of those who have none, an idea he thinks nearly confined to the sacred writings. Delitzsch ends with folly closing its mouth where the rest read iniquity; Wesley takes it for wicked men silenced, Gill for a poor man who, saved out of six troubles, hopes for the seventh.
17:
The blessing on correction opens the last movement. Clarke borrows the argument of Hebrews 12:5 about fathers of the flesh, and records that behold is absent from five of Kennicott's manuscripts and from the Vulgate. Ellicott thinks the line the original of Proverbs 3:12, and notes that its word for happy, the first word of the Psalms and used twenty-five times there, occurs nowhere else in this book. Wesley renders a plural, blessednesses, true only if everlasting blessedness is in view. Henry presses the prohibition three ways: against aversion, against contempt, against treating the stroke as chance. On the wounding Henry has a surgeon binding up the cut his own knife made, citing Caryl that God never makes a wound too deep for his own cure; Clarke prefers Coverdale, that though he make a wound he giveth a medicine again; Ellicott calls it one of those obvious sentiments which lose force by familiarity and then come home in sorrow with boundless power.

Six troubles and seven follow. Clarke takes the numerals for many: whoever delivered before will not withhold help now. Wesley explains the confidence historically: rewards and punishments fell more regularly then, and Eliphaz held great affliction certain evidence of wickedness, so deliverance must follow repentance. Ellicott finds the six-and-seven form characteristic of Proverbs, hears bitter irony because evil was already touching Job, and reads the next verse as past, he hath redeemed thee. Clarke passes on the Chaldee, which reads the chapter of Israel in Egypt, making the famine Egypt's, the war Amalek's and the tongue Balaam's incantation; his own note calls the tongue a world of fire kindled from the nethermost hell. Gill makes that scourge Satan the accuser or men's calumnies. Henry grants that not even the inoffensive can secure themselves against slander.

The league with the stones divides everyone. Clarke refuses Good's emendation of stones to sons for want of a manuscript, reports the Chaldee's covenant engraved on publicly erected tables of stone, then guesses at strongholds where banditti and chiefs kept, the promise being confederacy instead of raids like the Sabeans'. Gill keeps them literal: no hurt from walking barefoot among them, a crop from stony ground, boundary marks not to be removed. Wesley calls the figure bold and enlarges it, our covenant with God being one with all the creatures; Henry puts it the other way, a man at enmity with his Maker having the creatures at war with him. The clause about sinning parts the witnesses from the English. Clarke derives the word from erring and thinks mistake its sense here; Ellicott agrees, reading visit thy dwelling and miss nothing, a promise of not sinning sitting oddly beside inspecting a fold; Delitzsch has thou searchest thy household and findest nothing wanting.

Seed, grave and signature close it. Ellicott prefers numerous to great, then turns on the passage entire: a beautiful picture of the security of faith, vitiated by its want of correspondence with facts, Job's own case being the crucial instance and the problem too hard for his friends. Delitzsch works the philology, recalling Psalms 72:16, noting that offspring occurs only in Isaiah and Job, and that full age, found only here and at Job 30:2, answers an Arabic verb for being shrivelled with age, so meaning ripeness, matched by sheaves carried to the threshing-floor at harvest's end. Wesley calls it mercy to die seasonably, when the soul is ripe. Gill observes the grave is the house appointed for all living, and that none goes there but is carried. Gill and Wesley stress the corporate claim, no one man's conceit but what the friends had searched out. Ellicott will not let that pass: the boastful confidence is what is hard to bear, Eliphaz speaking as though Job's experience were nothing beside his own. Clarke agrees, calling the Temanite full of wise saws but miserably perverse in applying them.
